tweets.text:
A $100K/year customer gets white-glove treatment while a $10/year customer gets a help center. @DecagonAI's bet is that AI closes that gap, and enterprise is buying it.

Co-founders Jesse Zhang and Ashwin Sreenivas sit down with a16z's Kimberly Tan and Sarah Wang to discuss what they've learned running agents inside the biggest banks, airlines, and telcos:

- Smart-vs-cheap models are a false trade-off
- Start with frontier models on new use cases, then migrate to open-source after they mature
- Fine-tuning per use case works at the application layer
- Support demand always outran supply: make it cheaper and companies buy more of it

BREAKING: The Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) fell -3.8 million barrels last week, to 308 million barrels, the lowest since March 1983.

This marks the 18th consecutive weekly decline, the longest since 2023, per Zerohedge.

During this period, US oil reserves in the SPR have fallen -108 million barrels, or -26%.

Meanwhile, commercial crude oil stocks excluding the SPR dropped -7.2 million barrels, to 405 million barrels, the lowest since October 2018.

This is also ~7% below the 5-year average for this time of the year.

America's oil buffer is evaporating.

Zero-day options are now about 60% of all S&P 500 options volume.

Average daily volume hit a record 2.5 million contracts, up nearly fivefold in three years. Most of it expires worthless by the closing bell.

Here is the cost. When more than half the options market lives and dies in a single session, dealer hedging turns small moves into violent intraday swings. The next selloff comes faster and deeper than the fundamentals justify, and the buy-and-hold investor is the one who gets whipsawed.

Murata just raised its profit forecast 35% and warned the boom is ending in the same breath.

Murata makes the tiny ceramic capacitors packed inside every AI server. Its factories are running at 95% capacity, and it lifted its operating profit target to a record 380 billion yen.

Then its CEO said it plainly: the current pace of global tech infrastructure spending cannot hold.

When the picks-and-shovels supplier running flat out tells you demand is about to level off, the AI capex trade has a ceiling. The mega-cap names that priced in an endless buildout, the same ones carrying the S&P 500, are the first to re-rate when that spending flattens.

Here is how. The average selling price jumped 17% to a record $400. Companies are eating higher memory and component costs by charging the buyers who can still pay, and pricing everyone else out. Emerging-market volumes fell off a cliff.

This is the K-shaped consumer in one data point. The top trades up to premium, the bottom drops out entirely. Pricing power like Apple's keeps compounding. The mass-market names that sell to the buyer who just got priced out are the ones that bleed.

$AAPL

The largest pension fund in America is tearing up the standard investing playbook.

CalPERS manages $600 billion. Its new investment chief is moving to "total portfolio" investing, which means no more fixed buckets for stocks, bonds and private assets. Every dollar competes for the best risk-adjusted return instead of filling a quota.

Translation: the most sophisticated pool of retirement money in the country no longer trusts the rigid 60/40 model most people were handed. When the team running $600 billion stops drawing hard lines between asset classes, it is worth asking why you still do.

tweets.text: On this day in 1790, the U.S. government issued its very first patent, signed personally by President George Washington, to an inventor named Samuel Hopkins for an improved method of making potash, an industrial chemical used in soap, glass, and fertilizer. The patent system was written directly into the Constitution, which let Congress grant inventors exclusive rights to their discoveries for a limited time, on the theory that a temporary monopoly was a price worth paying to reward and speed up innovation. That first year, the government granted just three patents. The office Hopkins helped inaugurate has since issued more than 12 million, and the intangible assets it protects, patents, trademarks, and copyrights, now make up the majority of the market value of America's largest companies. Intellectual-property-intensive industries contribute over $7 trillion to U.S. GDP each year.
